seed.title: Seed phrase
seed.text: A list of English words, e.g. “olive tiger …”. You write it down on paper.

private.title: Private key
private.text: A huge number (256 bits long) calculated from the seed phrase. This is what signs your transactions.

public.title: Public key
public.text: Calculated from the private key with one-way maths (the same elliptic-curve method Bitcoin uses). Nobody can work backwards from it to the private key.

address.title: Address
address.text: The public key with a small label and a typo-check added, written out as letters and digits so it is easy to copy.

demo.minerPk: Public key of the miner of block <block>#{{height}}</block>
demo.computed: Address computed right here in your browser
demo.match: Matches the reward address recorded by the explorer.
demo.matchMiner: Matches the reward address recorded by the explorer ({{miner}}).
demo.noMatch: This miner receives rewards at a different address.

intro: An Ergo wallet doesn't actually “hold” ERG. Your ERG lives in boxes on the blockchain. What the wallet holds are the keys that open those boxes.

seed.title: From seed phrase to address
seed.p1: When you create a new wallet, everything is generated in a one-way chain:
seed.p2: Every arrow is a one-way calculation: easy going forwards, impossible going backwards. Someone who knows your address can't work out your private key. But someone who has your seed phrase has everything.
seed.figAlt: Seed phrase, private key, public key and address in a row, linked by one-way arrows. The seed phrase and private key are marked keep secret, the public key and address safe to share, and the way back is crossed out.
seed.figCaption: Each step can be computed from the previous one, but never the other way round: keep the first two secret, share the last two freely.

golden.title: The golden rule
golden.text: Your seed phrase is your money. Don't photograph it, don't store it in the cloud, don't send it to anyone — including people claiming to be “tech support”. Lose your seed phrase and your wallet together, and the money is gone forever; there's no bank to recover it for you.

nine.title: Why do Ergo addresses start with a 9?
nine.p1: A regular wallet address on Ergo mainnet looks like this: 9fQYeMEX…KSACVmgx. Regular wallet addresses always start with the digit 9; contract addresses can start with other characters.
nine.p2: Here's why. An address is really a short list of bytes turned into letters and digits (an encoding called Base58). The very first byte is a label (the prefix) that says which network the address is for (mainnet or testnet) and what type of address it is. The most common type — a normal wallet, called P2PK (Pay-to-Public-Key) — on mainnet has the prefix 0x01. When that byte, followed by the public key, is written out in Base58, the first character always comes out as “9”.
nine.p3: At the end of the address there are 4 more bytes: a checksum. If you mistype a single character, the checksum won't match and your wallet will refuse to send — protecting you from typos.

check.title: Check it yourself
check.p1: Every Ergo block contains the public key of the miner who found it. Below, this page takes that key from the latest block and computes the address itself — you can compare it with the address the miner uses to collect rewards:
check.p2: Want to dissect any address byte by byte? Use the <decoder>address decoder</decoder> or <pk>public key → address</pk> tools.

many.title: One wallet, many addresses
many.p1: From a single seed phrase, a wallet can derive many key pairs (using a standard called HD — “hierarchical deterministic” — the same one most Bitcoin wallets use), each with its own address. You can use different addresses for different purposes; your wallet balance is the sum of all of them. And all of them can be recovered from that one seed phrase.

contract.title: Not every address is a person
contract.p1:
Because a box's lock on Ergo can be a smart contract, some addresses represent a contract rather than a key. They are usually very long (the P2S type contains the entire script) and nobody “owns” them — only someone who satisfies the contract's rules can spend from them. See the
Addresses
article for details.

choose.title: Which wallet should I use?
choose.nautilus: Nautilus — a browser extension, used to connect to DeFi apps on Ergo.
choose.mobile: Ergo Mobile Wallet — an open-source mobile wallet for Android and iOS.
choose.satergo: Satergo — a desktop wallet that can run alongside a full node.
choose.p1: Whichever wallet you use, the principle is the same: you hold the seed phrase, you hold the money. Always download wallets from their official sources — the full list is at <list>ergoplatform.org/get-erg</list>.
